Vassilis Kapsambelis

Vassilis Kapsambelis

[kapsambelis@wanadoo.fr]

Vassilis Kapsambelis   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, and a Full Member of the Société psychanalytique de Paris. He was the general director of the ‘Association de Santé Mentale’ in the 13th district of Paris (2006-14) and is the current director of the Centre of Psychoanalysis of this institution. His works concern psychopathology and the treatment of psychotic and borderline pathologies, published in journals such as Revue française de Psychanalyse, Psychanalyse et Psychose, Revue française de Psychosomatique, Évolution psychiatrique. Among his publications (with titles given in English) are ‘The drugs of narcissism: Metapsychology of neuroleptics’ (1994), ‘Anxiety’ (2007), ‘The need of asylum: Places for psychoses’ (2011); he is also the editor of an academic publication, Manual of Clinical and Psychopathological Psychiatry of the Adult (Presses universitaires de France, 2018).
PSYCHOSIS, BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER, PSYCHOTHERAPY, PUBLIC MENTAL HEALTH, THIRDNESS, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE

The Centre for Psychoanalysis of the Mental Health Association in the 13th district of Paris is part of a community psychiatric public facility. It specializes in non-neurotic pathologies. The Centre offers several forms of psychoanalytic therapy for more than 200 patients, suffering from psychoses or severe borderline personality disorders. This double particularity of the Centre (public mental health facility and type of patients) has led it to develop distinct treatment techniques (for example, psychodrama) and to give special attention to the conditions of countertransference, as the demand for therapy is a challenge for both psychoanalysts and the psychiatric team who care for patients and refer them to the Centre. Over four decades, the analysts of the Centre have elaborated certain theoretical concepts (transference investment, thirdness and the ‘third person’, processual interpretation, ‘presence’ of the analyst, erotomaniac position …) that take into account the necessity of adapting the psychoanalytic approach to working with these categories of patients.

[[RunningHead]]

Rozsika Parker Prize 2019

The BJP's annual Prize, established in 2013 in memory of Rozsika Parker, focuses on a critical engagement with questions of creativity. An influential art historian and clinician, Rozsika Parker represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years and was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice. The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. It is expected that authors will address the question of creativity in their submission, however broadly conceived. This may be implicit or explicit. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should also consult the BJP's submission guidelines (particularly in relation to confidentiality, where clinical material is concerned) and prepare their work with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Student path is open to students on a training leading to a clinical qualification, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. A student paper may have been submitted as part of a course requirement, if this is acceptable to the student's course, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. A paper that has only been made available to an institution's membership (for example, in an internal bulletin) is eligible to be entered into the competition, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize, including length. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project. Manuscripts should be between 4000 and 6000 words in length including references, not including an Abstract of 200 words which should head the paper. The word length must be stated on the title page. The author's name should not appear anywhere in the body of the paper. If the paper is based on or makes use of the author's earlier published work this should be acknowledged in the form ‘(Author, date)’ within the text (i.e. the word ‘Author’ is given, plus date of publication) and there should be no entry in the References list. Manuscripts should be sent as a Word attachment to Ann Scott, Editor-in-Chief, c/o the BJP's Editorial Administrator bjpsychotherapyadmin@wiley.com

Remembering as Reparation: Psychoanalysis and Historical Memory by Karl Figlio. Published by Palgrave MacMillan, London, 2017; 284 pp, £65.00 hardcover, £22.99/$29.99 paperback

Jem Thomas

Jem Thomas

[jem.thomas@icloud.com]

Jem Thomas  

The Holocaust is, without doubt, the defining horror of our era, and the time that has elapsed since the end of World War II has not diminished the intensity with which it haunts our political and social preoccupations. Those 70 years have, however, also been years in which the Germans have sought to come to terms with that past. Their attempts to do so have also informed other attempts to deal with other traumas, other collapsed states and societies in communist Eastern Europe, apartheid South Africa, the legacy of dictatorships in Latin America and elsewhere. The task Karl Figlio has set himself in this important and scholarly work is a sustained reflection on what it means to remember, to memorialize and to try to make reparation. His book is about what Germans call Vergangenheitsbewältigung - overcoming the past. It is sometimes claimed that the Germans have done more, and done better, in seeking to make reparation, than others elsewhere. It is characteristic of Figlio to wonder if this ‘more and better’ does not conceal the very omnipotent triumphalism that was at work in the fantasies that sustained Nazism in the first place, making Germans what Jan-Werner Mueller sarcastically called, ‘world champions in remembrance’ (2010).

Karl Figlio is emeritus Professor of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies at the University of Essex and this book has all the scholarship one might expect from an internationally recognized academic. He has mastered literature on the Holocaust, on post-War Germany, on social theory and on psychoanalytic theory. The learning that has gone into this book is huge. Part of its importance comes from the fact that it is in the Palgrave book series Studies in the Psychosocial. The idea of psychosocial studies has emerged in recent years as an attempt to draw on psychoanalytic ideas to inform social research, including research methods, and, at the same time, to trace the social in the lineaments of the psyche.

Psychoanalytic Knowledge and its Production: Responding to Dreher, Briggs and Scott

R. Hinshelwood

R. Hinshelwood

[bob.hinsh@gmail.com]

R. Hinshelwood   Fellow of the British Psychoanalytical Society and a Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists. He is Professor Emeritus at the University of Essex, and previously Consultant Psychotherapist in the NHS, and Director of the Cassel Hospital. He is the Founder and Founder Editor of this Journal.

In the last issue of the journal, I wrote a short piece reflecting on my understanding of the place of research in the clinical setting (Hinshelwood, 2018). Three responses - from Anna Ursula Dreher, Stephen Briggs and Ann Scott in the same issue - did me the honour of engaging with my reflections.1 The Journal invited me to make a further response to these. So, I shall try to match their courtesy by taking as thoughtful a position as I can on their remarks.

As I understand it, Dreher was very much in agreement with an investigation of how much psychoanalysis can appeal to arguments similar to those in the ‘hard’ sciences. My previous work has tried to show that it is possible to shape a methodology that is at least science-like, even if it is not quite the ‘real’ thing. I used the word ‘parascience’ in my book Research on the Couch (Hinshelwood, 2013; see also Hinshelwood, 2018). But I also wonder if we should think of our work as knowledge-production, rather than claiming a full place at table with the physical sciences. There is no way around the fact that psychoanalysis2 is not a physical science. It may have a scientificity, but it is not a science of physical matter, and in that lies much of our troubles when we take our place amongst the other psychologies. The pieces I have written on this topic (Hinshelwood, 2008, 2013, 2018) have respected the headline alert that our ‘material’ is immaterial (Caper, 1988), it is subjective experience. As expressed in the quote from Glen Gabbard in my reflections in the last issue, our interest is the unique subjectivity of each individual person we see. It would seem appropriate to prioritize a research methodology that can preserve that subjectivity. So, when Dreher doubts our ability to match Karl Popper's model of natural science (Popper, 1959), I agree fundamentally with that doubt.

Nevertheless, my claim is that we should investigate whether a methodology that is science-like could be evolved - either along the lines I suggest, or some other lines. That seems to me critical for the future of psychoanalysis. The question is not so much about which psychoanalytic theories are ‘true’, though that is of importance. It is more to do with how we can make the assessment of truth, or at least the degree of validity a theory has in a particular clinical situation.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

bjp@ann-scott.net

Ann Scott  

In the last issue I mentioned that the BJP has always placed clinical narrative at its heart, and this issue begins with three such papers in our regular Clinical Practice and Theory strand. Each offers clinical immediacy; each locates its case material within a complex theoretical framework. Firstly, Jonathan Radcliffe and Frank Yeomans introduce and explicate Transference-focused Psychotherapy, adding to the theoretical literature on TFP - a modality underpinned by Kleinian object relations - with an extended case description. Importantly, for our comparative purposes, the TFP therapist ‘does not apply technical neutrality to behaviours considered inimical to the therapy. These are spelled out in a therapeutic contract negotiated before therapy can begin.’ The authors' detailed account - which covers contracting and the research evidence for TFP, among other themes - provides the reader with an opportunity to see TFP in practice, and to consider the question posed and thoughtfully discussed by the authors: ‘Could therapy have worked without behavioural injunctions?’

Next, Satoshi Handa describes work over several years with a hysterical patient, a survivor of severe abuse and neglect. Handa considers his countertransference at different stages of the treatment, in particular his great fear of his patient's death when she was absent without notice. Locating his work in both the classical and contemporary readings of hysteria, he looks at the ways in which he ‘enacted in her hysterical system’ and how he managed to disentangle himself from the enactment. He further argues that it is ‘essential to assess the extent of the hidden madness and fragmentation beneath the ostensible integrity’. His is a candid, thought-provoking discussion.

Thirdly, Mark J. Goldblatt, whose work on suicide has previously been published in the BJP, addresses the increasing use of assistance dogs by patients who suffer from a variety of psychological ailments: ‘as assistance dogs enter the physical space of the psychotherapist's office, we should consider their effect on the psychological space’, and in particular the intersubjective space. In the context of a comprehensive discussion of the nature and dynamics of work in this area, Goldblatt presents a clinical example involving a combat veteran with PTSD, major depressive disorder and suicidal ideation, whom he saw for treatment with his assistance dog. In an interesting discussion, Goldblatt suggests that ‘In some ways, the assistance dog acts like a co-therapist…. At other times, the assistance dog acts as a kind of supervisor, making real-time suggestions as to what will help reduce the patient's potential suffering’.

Olivia Humphreys   Radio producer and documentary filmmaker living in London. Her radio work has been broadcast on BBC Radio 4, BBC World Service, WNYC and ABC Radio National, and her films have been screened at over 50 festivals worldwide.
MOURNING, MOTHER, ANIMATED DOCUMENTARY, DREAMS, BABY

In this piece I describe the process of mourning my mother since her death in 2001, via my short animated documentary ‘Oneironauts - the Dream Travellers’ (2011) and my more recent experiences as the mother of a young baby. I consider my experience in the context of Freud's ‘Mourning and Melancholia’.

I enjoyed the privilege of being in conversation with Deborah Levy and this paper is a brief account of our dialogue. Deborah read from two of her novels, Swimming Home (2012) and Hot Milk (2016), and we discussed the points of contact between her writing and compositional process, reading her work and listening as a psychotherapist. She spoke of the importance of a back story and we thought about the way that history lies behind actions in the present, about the enduring impact of trauma and the transgenerational transmission of trauma.

Emma Letley

Emma Letley

[emma.letley1@gmail.com]

Emma Letley  

At a time when psychoanalysis is in the descendant and psychoanalytic publishing reducing its activities, Radical Psychoanalysis promises to be an important and valuable book in which Barratt argues passionately for a return to the discipline's roots (this is a key part of the ‘Radical’ title) in the free associative praxis; it is in the author's own words a plea ‘for a return to Freud's originality, in the interests of a wisdom that has been, over the course of the last century, obfuscated and all but lost’ (p. 2). The purpose of the book is to investigate the method of free association as the cornerstone of psychoanalysis. Barratt contends that despite the work of those such as Laplanche and André Green, to whom he pays homage, Freud's praxis of free association and the extent of his ‘Copernican’ revolution, have, in the main, been marginalized. The book expands on and elucidates his views as to why and how this is.

It is a pity that this outspoken and timely book is undermined by the author's unarguable erudition. I am not the only one to find his complexity difficult (Reppen, 2018). Without a careful reading of his earlier work, notably his book What is Psychoanalysis? (2012) and, at least, some of his papers (for example, Barratt, 2014), the text in this book, at times, verges on the inaccessible. Stylistically, Barratt's penchant for neologism, coinage and idiosyncratic locution drives the reader to take recourse in the dictionary.

I would put in a plea for greater simplicity of presentation, for some stringent editing, and copy-editing of the text. Sign of the times it may be to have minimal editing, but an edit to reduce repetition and obscurity would surely have been in order. This said, the book offers a compelling, if over-stated argument that psychoanalysis viewed as ‘a free associative praxis’ is much more radical, indeed ‘Copernican’, than has previously been considered. In putting forward his ‘manifesto’, Barratt privileges Freud's writings from 1896 to 1914: after that date, and particularly with the advent of World War I, his work became less focused on the revolutionary nature of his discovery of free association and more on re-centring the human condition. There is in Freud, and also in his descendants, a tendency to revert to more ‘Ptolemaic’ ways of thinking and modes of discourse - such discourse misses the concept of the repressed unconscious resulting ‘from the processes by which self-consciousness dispels contents from its own domain of representationality’ (p. 21).

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

bjp@ann-scott.net

Ann Scott  

‘I get drawn back into feeling we've achieved nothing, it's pointless, I'm wasting her time, I'm not good enough, she's stuck’, writes the author of the clinical material in this issue's Clinical Commentary. The patient is a woman in her fifties, initially referred ‘as her marriage was failing during infertility treatment’. We meet her when she has been in three-times weekly work on the couch for several years. Mark Budden and Ann Horne tell us, in introducing this richly rewarding piece, that all three commentators are qualified in both child and adult psychotherapy. This gives their comments a dual perspective, which encompasses both the developmental and the here-and-now of transference and countertransference, as well as the literature of both child and adult work.

We are delighted to publish the first article in our ‘New Voices’ section. The section has been carefully nurtured by Emma Letley and is designed, as we say in our Call for Papers for the section, to encourage writers to come forward - ‘new, early career writers, and those who may not yet have published but have significant experience to share with BJP readers’. Emma is working with a number of authors on the development of their papers and we expect to be presenting this work on a regular basis. (Readers may be interested to know that the papers, once ready for submission to the Journal, go through rigorous peer review and revision, as with all work published in the Journal.) In this issue, Anne Kane takes up the conscious and unconscious implications for disabled people of any change in the law on assisted suicide. As Kane acknowledges, assisted suicide is ‘not, in theory, specific to disabled people’, but ‘brings some of the psychosocial dynamics around impairment and disability into focus’. Making use of her significant experience and understanding of the field, she offers a thought-provoking and profoundly serious account of the topic.

We then turn to the work of one of the most distinguished contributors to our field: Jeremy Holmes. The BJP is privileged to have been approached to publish a group of papers from a two-day conference held in March 2018 in Exeter, ‘Peripheral Visions’, organized as a ‘Festschrift’ for Jeremy Holmes. The aim was to capture ‘the geographical, scientific, political and training implications of peripherality, and to celebrate his contribution to our discipline’, in the words of Mary Hepworth (formerly Target), who introduces the papers published here, and records the names and topics of the other speakers. As I looked through the topics of the conference as a whole, I was struck by how much they reflected a collegial way of working, often over many years, and by the extraordinary range of Jeremy's interests. The papers cover non-verbal communication between therapist and patient (Avdi and Seikkula), the portrayal of the ‘psy-professional’ in the media (Hopson); the possible negative effects of psychotherapy evidenced in the research literature and how these can be mitigated (Knox); threats to health provision from instrumentalism and linear thinking (Sarra); an attachment-informed psychoanalytic model viewed through a literary lens (Holmes himself).

‘Peripheral Visions’: A Conference Celebrating the Contribution of Jeremy Holmes and 20 Years of Psychoanalytic Studies at Exeter University, UK

Mary Hepworth PHD

Mary Hepworth

[m.hepworth@ucl.ac.uk]

Mary Hepworth  

The establishment of the psychoanalytic studies programme at the University of Exeter as a ‘periphery of excellence’ dates back two decades to an encounter in the North Devon Department of Psychiatry between two clinician-researchers: Eugene Mullan, a psychologist trained in cognitive analytic therapy, and Jeremy Holmes, a medical psychotherapist and champion of attachment theory and its clinical applications. Mutual commitment to open enquiry and psychotherapeutic ecumenicalism helped reconcile endemic rivalry between psychiatry and clinical psychology. They saw huge advantages, intellectual and administrative, in an academic rather than guild-based home for psychotherapy training. Coming from those different traditions, they nevertheless moved compatibly to the Psychology Department at Exeter University. Under the indefatigable and skilful aegis of Jungian analyst Richard Mizen, the programme has now matured academically from modest beginnings into a Masters and Clinical Doctorate, as well as encompassing multi-level psychoanalytic professional trainings.

Previously, would-be psychoanalytic psychotherapists in the South West had to travel long distances for training, with consequent depletion of local services. The accredited professional programme now covers the major psychoanalytic models, combining them with a rigorous enthusiasm for research. Attachment theory and, increasingly, relational neuroscience are strongly represented. Group analysis, psycho-sociology and organizational observation form a popular part of the programme. The virtues of questioning, democratic discussion and spontaneity are emphasized throughout.

‘Peripheral Visions’, a two-day conference in March 2018 organized as a ‘Festschrift’ for Jeremy Holmes by Richard Mizen, aimed at capturing the geographical, scientific, political and training implications of peripherality, and to celebrate his contribution to our discipline.

Each of the speakers picked up on aspects of Holmes’ enthusiasms. His US-based co-author, clinical psychologist and leading attachment researcher Professor Arietta Slade (Slade, 2016; Holmes & Slade, 2017) spoke of the importance of humanity and compassion in psychotherapists, an important Bowlbian theme. I had been fortunate to be an external examiner on the Exeter doctorate, and presented clinical work (Target, 2016) with a borderline patient, emphasizing the role - and some limitations - of psychoanalytic thinking and technique with such patients.

Postscript

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes

Jeremy Holmes  

Evolutionists (among whom I number myself) have trouble with grandparents. Post-reproduction, where's the selection pressure to maintain adaptation, or even life itself (Medawar, 1952)? The answer lies in inclusive fitness (Hamilton, 1964), that is, the ‘grandmother effect’. The persistence and know-how of post-reproductive elders improves the chances of their children's children's survival and flourishing. In hunter-gatherer societies grannies know where to forage for the best roots, while in AIDS-ravaged South Africa, grandparents ensure that their grandchildren survive even when both parents have succumbed. In economically - if not emotionally - developed societies, grandparents provide an essential backstop when parents are ill, separated, work-or poverty-stricken.

Grandparentally-speaking, I've now retired three times: from the NHS, from private psychotherapy practice (Holmes, 2018a), and the University - although I'm still (minimally) working. Each time, it's been good and bad. On the one hand, liberation and relief - hurrah, no more meetings! On the other, a sense of emptiness, of life slipping imperceptibly away: ‘was that it?’ As one of my patients put it, ‘what are you going to do without your weekly soap-opera?’ So when my friends and colleagues Richard Mizen and Nicholas Sarra generously offered to arrange a two-day ‘Holmes festschrift’ (or Peripheral Visions as I prefer to call it), I found myself, after a couple of half-hearted refusals, saying ‘yes’.

In the event it was exciting - if slightly terrifying. It was a wonderful opportunity to invite people who have mattered so much to me over the years, both in their own right, and as exemplars of the themes which have shaped my working life. Represented were: attachment-informed psychoanalytic psychotherapy (Arietta Slade and Mary Target), psychosocially minded general practice (Iona Heath), the society/psyche interface (Nick Sarra, Graham Music), evidence-based practice and practice-based evidence (Evrinomy Avdi, Jean Knox), international connections (Arietta and Evrinomy), the links between culture and psychotherapy, especially literature (Jackie Hopson, Jean), relational neuroscience and the Anna Freud Centre (Tobi Nolte, Mary and Graham).

[[RunningHead]]

Josephine Klein: 1926-2018

Josephine Klein, who died at the end of 2018 aged 92, was well known to many psychotherapists, who read her books, heard her speak or whom she taught. We first met in 1963 when I lived next to her at Nuffield, a postgraduate college for social scientists at Oxford University.

Josephine was formidably clever and widely read; she had gained two BA degrees in four years, in French at UCL, and then in Sociology at the LSE. But from the start she had been equally interested in practical action, having become involved in youth work and boys clubs. Her trenchant and personal style, in both speaking and writing, were to carry her out of academic life and into a long series of pioneering projects, among them the Archway venture in Brighton, the Community and Youth Work project at Goldsmith's College, and finally psychotherapy and the Refugee Therapy Centre. Her first books were on the theory and practice of working with groups, which she taught widely in universities and to a growing following of social and community workers. When we met she had just finished an important two-volume work, Samples from English Cultures (Klein, 1965). I focus on it because even now many of its lessons have not been learned.

At the time, sociology in Britain was dominated by the question of why working-class children were less successful in the educational system than their measured intelligence suggested. What Samples did was to create a cartography of social class in Britain; to relate together the existing studies of people in particular communities and occupations with what was known about their childrearing practices, how these affected their adult personalities and how they fared in life. Conscious of the limited and partial nature of the available data - which is why the book is called Samples - she outlined the extraordinary complexity of the English class system, whose rigidity and widespread influence had struck her very forcibly compared to her childhood in Holland. She raised important questions about how varied life chances are within social groups, between the sexes and over a lifetime. Nor, unlike many authors, did she idealize the educated classes; there is a pioneering comparison of the differences between the sort of conformist upbringing which produces successful senior professionals and civil servants, and the more energetic risk-taking characteristic of entrepreneurs.

Andrea Sabbadini

[a.sabbadini@gmail.com]

Andrea Sabbadini  

330

Born as a revolutionary form of therapy for the neuroses, psychoanalysis soon also became a psychological theory for the understanding of all sorts of cultural phenomena, the arts included. Early instances are Freud's own interpretations of a fictional work of literature (‘Delusion and dream in Jensen's Gradiva’, 1906) and of a sculpture (‘The Moses of Michelangelo’, 1914).

With a few notable exceptions (e.g. Milner, 1950; Kris, 1952; Gedo, 1983; Oremland, 1997), those who have written about the world of the arts from a psychoanalytic perspective have focused on art products rather than on the creative process involved in making them. Besides, most of such authors were either psychoanalysts without personal experience of creating art works, or art critics borrowing (and often misrepresenting) psychoanalytic ideas.

Desy Safán-Gerard, the California-based Chilean author of Chaos and Control: A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Unfolding Creative Minds, is an exception, being herself a visual artist also trained as a psychoanalyst, with considerable experience of working with creative patients from several fields. Prefaced by her first analyst Otto Kernberg, her book focuses on the different emotional components (both conscious and unconscious) involved in the creative process through a detailed observation of her own mind and body at work while painting.

The book consists of 16 chapters, neatly divided in two distinct parts: ‘Theories, conditions, and obstacles’ and ‘My own development’. This second section is richly illustrated with colour reproductions of many of her paintings and includes a sort of autobiographical trajectory of the author as an artist: from her early studies in music composition (and her ‘breakthrough’ encounter with Pierre Boulez and his music) to the development of her personal style as an abstract painter. Each page of her book conveys the impression that she approaches her painting activities with great passion - troubled at times, ecstatically joyful at others.

Catriona Wrottesley  

The creativity of Couple Stories is a fine demonstration of how, far from producing confusion and lack of conceptual clarity, the interplay of different analytic voices, each with a different approach to the same clinical material, enriches our thinking about couple relationships. Co-edited by Aleksandra Novakovic, psychoanalyst, psychologist, and couple psychoanalytic psychotherapist, and Dr Marguerite Reid, a consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist and couple psychoanalytic psychotherapist, the book's breadth of vision and understanding reflects the rich diversity of their respective professional backgrounds and trainings.

Divided into two principal parts, this volume opens with the section entitled ‘Mainly Theory’, which presents the reader with a solid platform of theoretical papers by Tavistock Relationships authors, Aleksandra Novakovic, Viveka Nyberg, Mary Morgan and Dr David Hewison. These papers explore core couple psychoanalytic ideas: love, hate and generosity, oedipal dynamics, projective identification processes and containment from an object relations approach and predominantly post-Kleinian perspective as developed at Tavistock Relationships over the past 70 years. This model considers the powerful unconscious forces at work in the couple relationship, and how the emotional and relational patterns, frequently ambivalent, uncertain and mistrustful, formed in early childhood, may be reactivated in the adult couple relationship, making it very difficult for the couple to find reflective space in their relationship in which to think about what is going on between them. This approach views the couple's relationship as the patient, and the focus of the therapist's concern.

The book's sequential arrangement of papers reflects a fundamentally post-Kleinian-informed theoretical model which views psychological development in terms of shifts and oscillations, from paranoid-schizoid states of mind to a more depressive state of mind in which concern for the other can be felt, together with an awareness of one's own destructiveness, and a wish to repair damage done to the other and the relationship (Chapter 1, Novakovic).

Anne Worthington  

Do not be seduced by the slimness of this volume and by Ricardo Cinalli's beautiful and startling illustrations into thinking that this publication is an ‘introductory’ text. Dr Welldon presents complex ideas that reflect her acclaimed expertise in sexual diversity and pathology, illustrated with clinical case histories from her forensic clinic, as well as from cinema and opera. Welldon's candid and anecdotal style provides the reader with a fascinating insight into her clinical style and practice.

This book is a timely reminder that there is nothing ‘natural’ about sex, sexual practices and sexual enjoyment. Unique to human subjectivity is the fact that sex is not merely a matter of reproduction and that sexual enjoyment has little or nothing to do with the satisfaction of drives. Much contemporary commentary might be interpreted as a disavowal of this, with sex situated within the discourses of health and entitlements. Welldon's clinical observations, case by case, along with the powerful drawings, emphasize that sex is not only about pleasure, but also about ‘pain and ultimately death’ (p. 90). Following Freud (1905), she argues that ‘unusual sexual practices’ [that] ‘evoke confusion … [so] that we respond with anxious or judgmental laughter’ are ‘completely unrelated to morality’ (p. 9). Her clinical vignettes illustrate how sexual practices, however bizarre, disturbing, anti-social or indeed criminal are not a matter of ‘ethics’ (p. 130) (by which she seems to mean morals), rather they function as a ‘mini survival kit’ (p. 131). Take, for example, her account of a man whose sexual satisfaction, from early adolescence, was only obtained by a total sensory deprivation obtained by ‘complicated rubber gear’ (p. 11) and who experienced uncontrollable sexual feelings in response to images of Houdini in a box. Welldon interprets his sexual practice as a need for a ‘second skin […] used as a protection against […] pain […] a container for anguish and anxiety of paramount proportions […] allowing him to maintain his appearance of being “normal”’ (p. 12). Furthermore, his difficult birth had meant that he had spent his early months in an incubator and thus ‘only a rigid box […] could offer a sense of survival’ (p. 14). Thus she reminds us that behaviours deemed ‘antisocial’ are deployed by some to defend against despair and as an attempt to regulate their experience of themselves.

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

It is always a special pleasure to publish the papers awarded the Rozsika Parker Prize, and in this issue we publish the three winning papers in the 2018 competition. Something about them – some quality that, to my eyes, the three papers shared, even though I could not quite put it into words - took me back to Margot Waddell's evocative Appreciation of Rosie in this Journal, following her death in 2010. In it Rosie was described as having ‘a particular quality of being … an unusually deep, creative and aesthetic appreciation of the dynamics of the therapeutic relationship’ (Waddell 2011, p.218). It was this ‘particular quality of being’ that led us to make questions of creativity the focus of the Prize in Rosie's memory; our three authors approach the question of creativity in the therapeutic relationship in a most thought-provoking way, each with its own ‘particular quality of being’.

Alexis Tomarken (Winner, Student Path) explores the experience of returning to a previous case, when a suicide in her own life brings her back to the suicide in her patient's life. She examines ‘how we cannot only alter our patients’ lives and future, but also how they can inform us of ours’, in ‘a complex entanglement of life histories of loss, current roles of caretaking, and future fears of what was to come in our lives.’

The Post-Qualification Prize was awarded jointly, to Guy Millon and Katya Orrell. Guy Millon argues that gender functions ‘as a fetish, screen or trick, that covers over traumatic loss’, an application of Lacan's theory of the gaze that designates all gender expressions as ‘modes of creative action’. His argument is developed by means of clinical material from three young trans patients. Katya Orrell, writing in a forensic context, addresses the psychic impact of an imprisonment for public protection sentence, ‘a sentence with no finite ending’. Using the concept of the swansong, ‘a song considered to be more beautiful because of the fragility of a life that is about to end’, she asks what is happening ‘when a prisoner whose unprocessed grief and rage threatens to destroy all creativity’.

Amita Sehgal  

This is a well edited volume that brings together the work of psychoanalysts and psychotherapists from Australia, China, Europe, Israel, Latin America and North America who are working psychoanalytically in their work with couples and families. The editors David E. Scharff (from Washington, DC, USA) and Elizabeth Palacios (from Zaragoza, Spain) have done an excellent job in weaving together a rich selection of clinical work that spans different cultures and diverse analytic orientations in such a way that it deepens our understanding of our clinical work. It also allows us, the reader, to become immersed in and engage with the different working styles employed by clinicians internationally.

By way of some background, this volume is the fifth in the series of books that form the Library of Couple and Family Psychoanalysis which was set up to publish the creative exchange of ideas and clinical practices around the world in the field of couple and family mental health. It is also the first book to emerge from several meetings of the International Psychoanalytical Association's Working Group on Family and Couple Psychoanalysis. This working group is made up of internationally distinguished couple and family psychoanalysts, and this book draws upon their ongoing research into comparative theories and methods of working analytically with couples and also with varyingly structured families.

The psychoanalysts and psychotherapists who have contributed to this book provide plenty of case material which they discuss through their particular theoretical frameworks. In doing this they potentially offer us, the reader, two types of experiences: firstly, we can get closer to understanding their thought processes whilst they are working; and, secondly, we can find ourselves sitting with them as they struggle with their patients, feeling and bearing the uncertainty of what will happen next.

The content of the book is organised around two main theoretical concepts that underpin the clinical presentations and form the framework within which these cases are understood and discussed. These are object relations theory, and the theory of the link (a theory that was first proposed by Enrique Pichon-Rivière in 1971). Pichon-Rivière was a naturalized Argentinian psychoanalyst whose thoughts about the experience of the individual as part of a group and a wider society overlapped but also intersected with those of Wilfred Bion, a British psychoanalyst. However, both psychoanalysts used the notion of the link differently.

Angela Foster  

I think this book is likely to receive mixed reactions; on the one hand it is a painstaking tour de force in the detail with which the author argues her case for the significance of the ‘site’ and the internalization of this in both psychotherapy and social work. Through providing multiple detailed clinical examples, which could be likened to process recordings, O'Neill carefully guides her reader through experiences of transition.

On the other hand, in framing her argument around the work of French psychoanalyst Jean-Luc Donnet and his emphasis on the ‘site’, O'Neill left this reader wondering why she had chosen this focus and what specifically it added to our understanding. The author states ‘Donnet designates the psychoanalytic setting in its broadest sense as the analytic “site”, composed of “elements” that can potentially be discovered and introjected, one by one, until the analysand's transformative discovery that he is in a functioning “analysing situation”. By this point, an analytic process is in train’ (Introduction, p. 1).

Is O'Neill in danger of underplaying the significance of other more familiar theoretical frameworks which also focus on the importance of the setting and the centrality of the relationship in establishing a therapeutic frame? For example, Winnicott's focus on the ‘holding environment’ (not mentioned), and Bion's writing on the ‘container/contained’ (only fleetingly referenced)? Both these theoretical perspectives, derived from hypotheses about early childhood, although differing in emphasis, seek to identify how therapeutic change is facilitated through experience. Reference is made to Winnicott's notion of ‘created/found’, linking it with Freud's papers on technique, referring, I believe, to free association. O'Neill writes: ‘In Donnet's view, the enunciation of this “fundamental rule” of psychoanalysis establishes the treatment as a tabula rasa that the patient will write on, a pristine terrain in which, as the patient sets foot in it for the first time he paradoxically finds/creates, in Winnicott's sense, his own analysis. It is the opportunity for the patient to utilise the analytic situation that is all-important’ (p. 26). It is difficult to see what exactly it is that Donnet adds to the more familiar theories of Freud, Winnicott and Bion.

Rosemary Rizq   Professor of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy at the University of Roehampton, London, UK. She is a psychoanalytic psychotherapist accredited with the UK Council for Psychotherapy and a counselling psychologist registered with the Health and Care Professions Council, chartered with the British Psychological Society. Until recently, she worked as Adult Psychotherapist at Forest House, a specialist NHS psychoanalytic psychotherapy service. ANATHEISM, FAITH, FICTION, LITERATURE, PSYCHOANALYSIS, WAGER, WINNICOTT

Colm Tóibín's novella The Testament of Mary (2013) offers a provocative re-imagining of the Virgin Mary's life 20 years after the crucifixion of her son Jesus. Drawing on Richard Kearney's notion of anatheism or a ‘return to God after God’, I use the fictive space opened up in Tóibín's version of the Gospel as a spur to understanding the way in which faith may be conceived of as wager within both fiction and psychoanalysis. Discussing how the reception of the artistic message requires the same spirit of hospitality as does the encounter with alterity within the psychoanalytic relationship, I argue that in both cases we are faced with an existential moment of choice that requires a wholehearted willingness to engage with otherness. The implications of Tóibín's story for psychoanalytic work are then explored with reference to developmental processes outlined by Winnicott (1971) in his paper ‘The use of an object’. The paper concludes with a brief discussion of the significance of testimony within psychoanalytic work.

Dear Editor,

I would like to bring to the readers' attention the publication of the 8th volume of Ma'arag: The Israel Annual of Psychoanalysis.

Ma'arag (“weave, web, fabric” in Hebrew) is a Hebrew-language (English abstract), academically-refereed journal brought forward by a consortium of The Sigmund Freud Center for the Study of Psychoanalysis of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and 9 of Israel's chief psychoanalytic institutes, associations and groups: The Israel Association for Self Psychology and the Study of Inter-subjectivity, The Israel Society for Analytical Psychology, The Israel Psychoanalytic Society, The Israel Association for Group Analysis, The Israel Institute of Jungian Psychology, The Tel-Aviv Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis, The Israel Association for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, The Israel Association of Psychotherapy, and The Winnicott Center in Israel. The annual is published by Magnes/The Hebrew University Press of Jerusalem. I have edited the previous 8 volumes of Ma'arag (2010-2019), and am succeeded by Professor Dana Amir of Tel-Aviv University and the Israel Psychoanalytic Institute. Prof. Gaby Shefler of the Hebrew University and the Israel Psychoanalytic Institute chairs the Editorial Board. The profession of psychotherapy has a richer tradition of literature on theory than on technique and still less exists in the vein of how to go about building a practice. It is therefore most welcome to see the publication of this detailed and candid book by Brett Kahr, How to Flourish as a Psychotherapist, in which he provides the reader with a comprehensive and revealing description of how to build and maintain a successful psychotherapy practice. In his introduction, Kahr acknowledges the contribution made by Nina Coltart in her book How to Survive as a Psychotherapist (1993) and states his aim to explore what allows a psychotherapist to flourish rather than simply survive. In doing so he communicates enthusiasm, dedication and a tremendous breadth of interest, offering copious insight and advice, which is always welcome in a profession that can seem mysterious due to its confidential nature. Kahr, like Coltart before him, never pretends to offer anything other than a very personal view of the profession. This is neither a researched topic nor a manual, but rather takes the form of a collegial sharing of experience that at times is like a memoir. He also shows a similar spirit of generosity in the way he shares so much of his early career, including the difficulties encountered on the way. In lively conversational style he offers fascinating and humorous scenarios and anecdotes from different stages of his career. One such example is his experience of addressing an audience of two in a Jewish women's book group in Golders Green: ‘Addressing the United Nations’ (p. 114).

Kahr presents a developmental model based on his own life-time journey from his starting point as a nervous, but dedicated, undergraduate, and he gives the sense of having evolved through his work like an artist who develops and improves with age. Drawing on his own experience and that of his colleagues and students, he charts the path from pre-training, through training, starting up a practice, building a reputation, and challenging oneself to step into a public arena by taking on projects of writing, public speaking and research.

At a time when the polarities of victim and aggressor, good folks and bad folks, and guilty and innocent seem to be the only available categories with which to classify human action, it is perhaps all the more urgent to find alternative ways of thinking about questions of agency, motivation and classification. In her long and remarkable career, Estela Welldon has done precisely this, challenging received opinions about trauma, abuse, perversion, criminality and motherhood, and encouraging us to reflect on what drives people to behaviour that we can all too easily dismiss, condemn and vilify.

This new collection of essays celebrates her work, and shows the many ways in which she has transformed the field not only of forensic psychotherapy but of related areas of analytic thought and practice. In this, Welldon continues the tradition of Freud, who urged caution in our kneejerk reactions to violence and crime, and a proper exploration of the meaning and the function of the so-called criminal act. Just as Freud revealed how violence may be linked to an underlying guilt, Welldon has focused on the early history of the individuals involved, and how their actions may be seen not only as aspects of the compulsion to repeat but as efforts to heal themselves and distance the malign forces they experience internally.

Welldon's work here and her celebrated vitality and passion for transmitting her ideas have led to the creation of the first formal training in forensic psychotherapy at the Portman Clinic, as well as the foundation of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy. This has not been simply a grouping of those interested in psychotherapeutic approaches to forensics, but also a battle against the societal and institutional forces which favour punishment to understanding. Even analytically oriented practitioners were often hostile to her approach, which saw her insisting that therapy groups include both perpetrators and victims, resisting exactly the polarization that her work has always tried to analyse rather than perpetuate.

This paper uses a personal clinical example from my practice to demonstrate the complexities and nonlinearity of time in a discussion of unconscious entanglements. These entanglements include personal intersections of my patient's history and mine, events at the time of our meeting, and the unknown future. These entanglements become uncanny, and in the uncanny what is revealed is not only illuminating but altering. This detailed and intimate examination of how we cannot only alter our patients' lives and future, but also how they can inform us of ours, provides a platform to discuss the mutual vulnerability of both patients and analysts. Despite the creative engagement and transformation that can take place in these discussions, we as analytically minded therapists continue to struggle to share this autobiographical piece of our work with each other.

It was a remnant of the hypnotic method and a way of sparing himself the patient's gaze; it was ‘a certain ceremonial … to isolate the transference and to allow it come forward’ (Freud, cited on p. 7). REPRESENTATION, PARADOX, LANGUAGE, EXPERIENCE, SYMBOLIZATION, TRANSITIONAL OBJECT, CHILDREN'S LITERATURE, CREATIVITY

Creativity is connected to our experiences. But how are these represented in language? The concept of paradoxical representation is introduced here as a ‘solution’ to this problem. Two other solutions are focusing on the non-representational and creating a ‘private’ language. Psychoanalysis and children's literature use these solutions in order to deal with representation of the ‘inner world’. However, when using paradoxical representation, the way in which this world is represented is unique. This is so because the relationship between language and experience is truly paradoxical in nature. It presents two different and contradictory manners of representation - one in which the word symbolizes - and does not symbolize - the experience; one that is separate - and not separate - from it; and one that serves as subjective expression and public communication. This representation is one in which successful representation, which symbolizes the thing, is a representation that fails, and therefore does not symbolize it. Although creativity can also stem from non-verbal realms or from ‘private’ languages, using words as paradoxical representations - which in Winnicottian terms means using words as transitional objects - maximizes the creative process and is thus the ‘royal road’ to creativity.

This paper presents a case study that aims to further our understanding of the relational and embodied aspects of the psychotherapy process. One psychoanalytic session is examined on multiple levels, including talk, participants’ physiological arousal and interactional attunement, ruptures in the therapeutic alliance, postural congruence and facial expression of affect. Implicit processes of non-verbal attunement seem to play a role in resolving ruptures and in fostering exploration and the creation of new meanings. Embodied attunement was found to be at its highest at points in the session characterized by verbal disjunction and ruptures in the therapeutic alliance. The therapeutic dyad was ‘in sync’ non-verbally until tension was resolved, at which point, synchrony was relaxed, and therapist and client were able to proceed with their respective ‘tasks’, secure in the knowledge that the other is there for them. It is argued that attempts to describe the complex and nuanced processes of psychotherapeutic change would benefit from attending to both explicit/semantic and implicit/non-verbal domains of interaction.

Female sexuality and especially the nature of female orgasm has been a highly contested area, both within and outside psychoanalysis. Throughout the ages, and despite the efforts of many campaigners, female sexual pleasure, if any is allowed for at all, has been tightly tied to reproductive aims and functions, in many ideologies and discourses. Sexual liberation and reform movements of many kinds have consistently tried to re-evaluate the importance of the clitoris to female pleasure and orgasm, and to question the purported role and ideological dominance of the vagina and vaginal orgasm in ideals of femininity and heterosexual pleasure. As Zachary points out, and many authors before her have said, the clitoris has constantly been discovered, then disappeared, then rediscovered; an interesting example of disavowal and denial in the cultural history of purportedly scientific knowledge about contested subjects. What to this reader is welcome about this book, is the description of allegedly recent anatomical knowledge that might have a progressive and helpful role in advancing women's and men's understanding of the clitoris, its intricate connections to the surroundings of the vagina, and its centrality to sexual pleasure for many women. As Zachary says, knowledge about the body may change and this must affect the psychic representation in our minds - anatomy is not a complete given.

What is less clear - because only relatively old diagrams are provided - is whether the knowledge that Zachary argues is so recent and so ground-breaking is in fact that new. Certainly younger readers, not subject to the tyranny of the dominant myth of the vaginal orgasm, so effectively challenged by feminists (whom Zachary barely mentions, and then only to misrepresent and criticize), the researchers Masters and Johnson, and many in the sex therapy world, might feel this is largely old news, or common knowledge, at least for some. However, the clitoris is really only the topic of a few chapters. The others are entitled: ‘Womankind throughout history’; ‘Bisexuality: A universal phenomenon’; ‘Motherhood: The fundamental aim’; ‘Femininity: The key to the box’; ‘Aggression and the female form’; some of which are previously published papers or conference talks, and all of which range sketchily over very large topics.

ASSISTED SUICIDE, DISABILITY, IMPAIRMENT, TRAUMA, LOSS, MOURNING, CONTAINMENT, FACILITATING ENVIRONMENT, NARRATIVE, PSYCHOSOCIAL, SOCIAL MODEL

This paper explores the issue of assisted suicide in relation to disabled people from a psychosocial perspective. The implications, particularly the unconscious implications, for disabled people and for the psychosocial dynamics around disability if assisted suicide was made lawful in the UK are explored. Assisted suicide is the subject of persistent attempts at legal change and while not, in theory, specific to disabled people, the issue brings some of the psychosocial dynamics around impairment and disability into focus, illuminating the attitudes and emotions with which disabled people must try to live. Psychoanalytic ideas in relation to trauma, loss, mourning and containment are drawn upon with particular reference to the work of Freud, Klein, Bion and more contemporary thinkers such as Garland, Sinason and Rustin. The paper draws on three texts by disabled people in order to explore emotional responses to profound impairment. Attachment theory helps in considering varying narrative styles. Disability studies literature and legal, social and political contextual issues inform the psychosocial perspective applied in the paper.

Jeremy Holmes MD FRCPsych

Jeremy Holmes

[j.a.holmes@btinternet.com]

Jeremy Holmes   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist and Visiting Professor at Exeter University. His most recent books are The Therapeutic Imagination: Using Literature to Deepen Understanding and Enhance Empathy (Routledge 2014) and Attachment in Therapeutic Practice (with Arietta Slade, SAGE 2017).
ATTACHMENT, PSYCHOANALYSIS, LITERATURE, ADOPTION, EMPATHY

The paper proposes Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale (WT) as foundation narrative for attachment-informed psychotherapy, and a counterpart to Oedipus Rex (OR), covering similar psychological territory but in a strikingly different way. Both start with a father's rejection of a baby and its rescue and adoption by distant shepherds. Both revolve around murderousness and desire in a mother-father-child triangle, but in WT the prime mover is filicide rather than parricide. WT points to the positive aspects of the care-giving dynamic. The main characters of WT, in contrast to OR's phallocentrism, are the rejected Queen Hermione, her handmaiden Paulina and Perdita herself. Their relationships are characterized by attachment security: this gives Paulina the courage to confront and instigate mentalizing in Leontes, the psychotic king, and for Perdita to find her sexuality through her transgressive love for Florizel. The environmental benefits of adoption are highlighted as WT's tragi-comic dynamic moves from chaos to renewal and rebirth: Hermione survives the ‘attack on the good object’; Leontes recovers from his jealous hatred and subsequent depression; ruptures are repaired. WT depicts secure attachments as bulwarks against loss, and the key to resilience in the face of trauma.

Jan Hepburn  

This wide-ranging book aims to offer a way of thinking about our current and historical social trends through the lens of psychoanalytic theory and insights. The author aims to offer a psychoanalytic understanding of some of the current preoccupations of our social world, particularly where polarization and polemics dominate the political landscape. He uses a variety of sources and writers to both explore and evidence his ideas; from Alderdice to Žižek though Arendt, Britton, Freud, Kafka, Lear, Rosenfeld, Sinatra, Volkan and many others. Complex concepts are explored and examined and linked with the author's underlying ‘integrated psychoanalytic perspective’ (p. xv).

The first chapter weaves psychoanalytic theory into structural and sociological understandings about the human condition post the industrial revolution. This is followed by three chapters looking at narcissism, embodied experience and social groups, all moving between psychoanalytic understandings, criticisms of them and other theoretical positions to try to offer a framework into which the reader can put some apparently disparate concepts. For the reader, this can be an exhilarating but at times a slightly confusing journey. However, by the end of Chapter 4 it is becoming clear that the understanding of human behaviour and social trends has to include both internal and external factors, and that what has gone before is often decisive in what happens next. Just as taking a full history in a clinical situation (sadly now the rather old fashioned practice) is central to the understanding of the patient's here-and-now predicament, the next five chapters are concerned with our history and trying to understand our here-and-now social predicament. These chapters unravel various writers’ contributions to the struggle to gain purchase on the slippery areas of destructive narcissism, nationalism and Nazism and knitting them back up into the psychoanalytic overview of how these things may be understood.

By the end of Chapter 9 the author has made the argument that what happened in the western world post the Second World War was ‘the end of history’ (p. 75). This phrase encompasses something both emotional and structural which has resulted in a discourse in which, he argues, individualism has triumphed over the common good, and what could be learned from history is denigrated and disregarded. The author identifies five contributing factors to this regrettable state of affairs - economic changes, globalization, moving away from liberal values of fairness, the loss of respect for history and individual alienation.

Katya Orrell

Katya Orrell

[katya.orrell@panoptikon.uk.com]

Katya Orrell   A psychodynamic psychotherapist trained at the Tavistock Clinic. She is a director and founding partner of Panoptikon, an organization working with offenders and prison staff. She is winner of the 2017 British Psychoanalytic Council PP Now Award for Innovative Excellence. She is secretary of the Forensic Psychotherapy Society, a board member of the International Association for Forensic Psychotherapy, and is currently the Ethics and Professional Standards representative for the Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists. She works individually with clients in private practice and the NHS, and her work involves training, consultancy and research. She teaches, has presented at international conferences and is currently editing a book on prison experience.
IPP SENTENCE, DESTRUCTIVENESS, APRÈS COUP, SWANSONG COMPLEX, TRANSIENCE, CREATIVITY, GRIEF, HOPE

Chekhov's play Swansong could be describing a prison wing. Depicting a drunk, elderly comic actor who has fallen asleep after the performance is over and awaking to a deserted theatre, he speaks, and is answered by the prompter responding from the darkness, an image not unlike the therapeutic dyad. Over recent years, working psychodynamically in a man's prison has felt dangerous. For someone serving an imprisonment for public protection (IPP) sentence, a sentence with no finite ending, the threat of psychic death, of hope, is the sword of Damocles which hangs over his every day. I examine what it means to undertake clinical work with a man who never knows when he will leave prison. Using the concept of the swansong, a song considered to be more beautiful because of the fragility of a life that is about to end, I ask what is happening when a prisoner whose unprocessed grief and rage threatens to destroy all creativity. I explore how the danger of his internal destructiveness meets and is reflected by the actual threat of our extinction as forensic psychotherapists. What happens to the ability to contain, when the relationship with the prison itself feels dangerous, when each session feels like our swansong?

Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz

Dorothée Bonnigal-Katz  

After the incredible success of the 2016 Psychosis and Psychoanalysis Conference at the Freud Museum – the British Journal of Psychotherapy published all the papers in a wonderful double edition (2017) – it seemed that a sequel was in order: the interface between psychoanalysis and psychosis deserved more examination across politics, technique, theory, and history. Hence this second conference, in September 2018, which gathered an impressive panel of frontline clinicians bringing their extensive experience of working psychoanalytically with psychosis – a rare feast for anyone interested in the subject. All the papers presented at the conference are published in this and the next issue of the British Journal of Psychotherapy, except for Berjanet Jazani's paper ‘Psychotic politics: A fury road to the awakening of the primal Father’, which will be included in her forthcoming book.

I was personally enthralled by the clinical and theoretical vibrance of the day. From attachment theory to the French tradition, from Freud and Lacan to Gisela Pankow and Winnicott, from the collective to the individual, from institutions to the community, a variety of perspectives, approaches and settings were discussed and explored in depth. The speakers all gave us fascinating insights into their clinical engagement with psychosis and their personal contribution to the field, leaving us at once inspired and unsettled, hopeful and troubled. In the uncertain times in which we live when, as Freud already observed in 1938, ‘we find to our astonishment that progress has allied itself with barbarism’ (1938, p. 54), the fate of the most vulnerable members of our society is more precarious than ever. In this ‘remarkable period’, to carry on quoting Freud, how to uphold a viable safety net and support system beyond crippling differences and hierarchies perhaps remains the most urgent question.

This conference is inscribed in a fruitful partnership with the Freud Museum London and collaborating with them was, once again, an absolute pleasure; I thank them warmly for their generous support, especially Ivan Ward and Stefan Marianski. I also thank Ann Scott and the British Journal of Psychotherapy

This paper discusses the benefits and the challenges of running a specialist psychoanalytic project in the community in the current economic and political climate. As the founder and clinical lead of the Psychosis Therapy Project, an Inner London service for people who experience psychosis, the author reflects on the pitfalls currently facing the psychoanalytic treatment of psychosis and exposes the ideological violence underlying the dominant model of recovery and rehabilitation in mental health care. Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

bjp@ann-scott.net

Ann Scott  

This issue of the Journal opens with a situation that may be easily recognizable in our clinical work, taking into account, of course, the uniqueness of the individual case: an ‘intractable refusal to do what would be needed to grow’. Our Clinical Commentary author presents work with a 21-year-old male student whose father died suddenly when he was three years old. The young man ‘seemed very stuck, not getting any of his college work done, while buying off his tutors (and trying to buy off himself and me) with promises’. The therapist sees their job as being to ‘excavate the desperation below the surface’ of the intractable refusal. It would be impossible to summarize the complexity of the commentators’ responses to this engaging, candid account, but some key observations stand out: the idea of ‘a deficit in his relationship with himself which needs to be repaired’ (Richard Carvalho); the suggestion that we are seeing ‘a defensive system crumbling…exposing the traumatic burden of grief which has been obscured for so long’ (Jane Cheshire); a focus on the developmental, with the patient ‘longing to have had a vigorous active father with whom he could identify’ (Meg Errington).

When the judges and I read the work submitted for the Rozsika Parker Prize each year, our focus is always on the question of creativity - whether this be creativity of topic, or creativity of expression; in all cases, whether we are seeing the new, the unexpected, the different. It is naturally a pleasure to publish the two Commended papers in the 2018 competition, both in the Post-Qualification Path. In a sensitive, imaginative account, Toby Ingham considers the power of remembered nightmares to ‘aid work and understanding’, particularly where the history may have been traumatic, with much that has been forgotten. Naftally Israeli, in a closely argued, subtle treatment of paradoxical representation, addresses ‘two disciplines that place special emphasis on creativity and the inner world - psychoanalysis and children's literature for the very young’, noting that both deal with birth: ‘the birth of words from experiences, and the birth of experiences from words’.

Countertransference and Alive Moments: Help or Hindrance by R. D. Hinshelwood. Published by Process Press, London, 2016; 286 pp, £19.95 paperback

Michael Halton

Michael Halton

[mi.halton@btinternet.com]

Michael Halton  

Hinshelwood is a prolific writer and we owe him a large debt of gratitude for his many papers and books, in particular two earlier volumes, A Dictionary of Kleinian Thought (1989), and Clinical Klein (1994). Both books are clear and lucid accounts of Kleinian and post-Kleinian developments in theory and clinical technique, and have been of enormous use in bringing what are difficult and sometimes arcane ideas to a wide audience.

This new book on countertransference is partly the summary of many previously published papers on the subject and shows some of the same impressive scholarly inclinations as his earlier work. It has a very helpful review of the key theoretical ideas as well as extensive accounts of the range of clinical phenomena related to countertransference. There is a good summary of the subject as it is described in the literature and how it is considered from within the different schools of psychoanalysis. However, it suffers from a surprising lack of an index.

The title Countertransference and Alive Moments with its subtitle Help or Hindrance perfectly captures the central issues that arise from the study of countertransference and which inform the contemporary practice of psychoanalysis as a clinical method. The ‘Alive Moments’ of the title refers to the heart of the matter. The essential emotional aspects of any contact between therapist and patient, that are fresh and immediate, are now understood to underpin any intervention that has a real mutative outcome. Hinshelwood argues very persuasively that it is around these alive moments that the claims of psychoanalysis as a method for psychic change, rests.

‘Help or Hindrance’ covers the controversies that still abound around the use and misuse of countertransference as a source of information about the transference. On this point it is interesting to compare Hinshelwood's detailed discussions with another recently published book of hitherto unpublished lectures and seminars that Klein herself gave to candidates in training at the British Psychoanalytical Society in 1936 and 1958 respectively. These lectures and seminars were discovered in the Klein Archives and remained there until their editor John Steiner brought them together in book form (2017).

Susan Kegerreis

Susan Kegerreis

[skeger@essex.ac.uk]

Susan Kegerreis  

In this volume, Prophecy Coles sets out to bring the dynamics around step-parenting out of what are asserted to be the shadows, to explore the origins of some of the myths which colour experiences in step-families and to establish the importance in therapeutic work of appreciating the power and enduring influence of step-relationships. It calls on ancient and more recent literature, fictional, biographical and of the self-help variety, in support of its arguments, and it represents a great deal of relevant and interesting scholarship in these areas.

The bulk of the early part of the book concentrates on the origins of mythology around the step-mother role and our cultural characterization of it. Coles shows how psychoanalytic theorizing (e.g. Bettelheim, 1976) has generally focused on how folk tales work at an unconscious level to elucidate internal dynamics. She argues that psychoanalysis has thereby overlooked the real social dynamics that the tales are bringing to our attention and has ignored their role in informing children (and adults) about actual family anxieties and concerns.

This follows a line already evident in Coles’ work - the emphasis on the wider influences on individual psychic development. She has written elsewhere effectively and innovatively about sibling dynamics and about the role of wet-nurses and nannies, arguing strongly that the core psychoanalytic focus on the nuclear mother/father/infant relationship has led to an underestimation of how vital the wider world is in its effect on the young child's internal dynamics. In this she joins a wider chorus of voices (e.g. Frosh, 2013; Hopper, 2011) pointing out that social systems and ideas about the social unconscious need to be incorporated into psychoanalytic thinking. It is no longer, if it ever was, sufficient to think about the inner world as being contingent only on the individual family dynamics and internal oedipal struggles, as we become ever more aware of unconscious dynamics which are of much wider origin.

Tom O'brien   Clinical social worker and psychotherapist with more than 40 years of practice, in both private practice and mental health services. He works in Child and Youth Mental Health and as a Senior Lecturer in the School of Medicine, University of Queensland, Brisbane.
PEER SUPERVISION GROUP, GROUP ANALYSIS, PSYCHOSOMATICS, PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, RESEARCH METHODS

This paper reports on the work of a peer supervision group engaged in simultaneous research and clinical supervision. During an 18-month period, the group met to discuss 22 individual treatments of people diagnosed with psychosomatic disorders to identify common patterns of resistance and to assist therapists to effectively manage resistance. The aim of the present study was to identify and better understand psychological challenges the group experienced during this research process and its impact on their capacity to work effectively in their tasks. Supervision meetings were recorded and two types of qualitative analyses, derived from the work of Pichon-Rivière and Bion, were performed to study the group work and processes. Analysis showed fluctuations and compromise formations between the tendency to work objectively and to regress during critical periods of the research process. Factors that pulled the group in both directions are identified and discussed. We believe many of the processes observed in this study are applicable to other peer supervision groups. An understanding of such group processes is likely to enhance group work.

CHILDHOOD NIGHTMARES, REMEMBERED CHILDHOOD DREAMS, CRAFT OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, CLAUSTROPHOBIA, CORE COMPLEX

This essay explores work with adult clients who have a particular attachment to their childhood nightmares. The essay argues that in the remembered nightmares, we have access to particularly well preserved dynamics and memories that can aid work and understanding. It is interesting that in cases where so much may have been forgotten, particularly in cases that involve trauma, memories of these dreams have endured. There is the somewhat tragic sense that some of the problems that have gone on to trouble the client's life were visible in the nightmares, and there to be addressed all those years ago. How different a life might have been if the issues in the childhood nightmares had been addressed at the time when they were first dreamt. The essay pursues the idea that remembered childhood nightmares can supply us with, firstly, important information that can support understanding of clinical work; and secondly, the possibility of assisting someone in carrying out work that has been long neglected.

Emma Letley

Emma Letley

London
[emma.letley1@gmail.com]

Emma Letley  

Creativity is a fraught topic for psychoanalytic writers and theorists: a recent book by Donald Moss is one example with its searching discussion of creativity and its ‘fetishization’ (Moss, 2018). Freud wrote extensively about individual artists and works of art but did not engage with the artistic process itself. Classical theory, following Freud's view of the arts as a neurotic configuration, tends to pathologize the process and, at times, to prioritize the Kleinian view of creative work as, largely, driven by the wish to repair. A key, underlying question posed by Townsend's book is: can psychoanalysis throw light on art without reducing it?

It is an original contribution to questions such as this, filling a gap in theorizing about art and doing so with conscientious attention to detail and respect for the interviewees and their individual process and achievement. Townsend has the advantage of being both clinician and artist, and her use of her own work is both generous and illuminating. She offers us a compelling account of the artistic process, employing interviews with 33 artists, from the point of view of the Independent Tradition where an interest in creativity is a hallmark. The book is underpinned by the work of Milner, Bollas and Winnicott as well as that of thinkers relevant to but outside the psychoanalytic arena, such as Anton Ehrenzweig and Susanne Langer.

Chapter 1 puts forward and develops Townsend's notion of the ‘pre-sense’, that is the artist's initial experience of sensing the potential of something external, be it a feature of landscape, a fabric or a photograph. Chapters 2 and 3 look at the period of gestation when little appears to be happening at a time before the form of the work comes to light. The author draws on her own experience of a work's early stages as well as that of a photographer and other artists, usefully referencing Bollas' (1992) notion of the ‘receptive unconscious’.

Stijn Vanheule   Clinical psychologist and professor of psychoanalysis and clinical psychological assessment at Ghent University, Belgium, where he is the Chair of the Department of Psychoanalysis. He is also a psychoanalyst in private practice (Member of the New Lacanian School), and the author of numerous journal articles and books, including The Subject of Psychosis: A Lacanian Perspective (2011) and Psychiatric Diagnosis Revisited: From DSM to Clinical Case Formulation (2017).
LACAN, SUPERVISION, SUPERAUDITION, PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, LANGUAGE

Supervision is crucial to most forms of talking therapy. This article focuses on psychoanalysis and explores how supervision can be conceptualized from a Lacanian point of view. We discuss two principal ideas about supervision from Lacan's work: making the analyst sensitive to the symbolic component of the unconscious and becoming sensitive to the interrelation between language and jouissance. These ideas comprise two stages that Lacan discerned in the process of supervision: the ‘stage of the rhino’ and the ‘stage of the pun’. We illustrate Lacan's distinction between these stages by means of vignettes of analysts who were supervised by Lacan. We argue that an additional third stage should be discerned, concerning the challenge of incarnating the position of the so-called object a. Last, we discuss the pitfalls that an analyst might experience when conducting and directing the analytic work, namely the consistency of the imaginary, the delusion of the symbolic and the real of the body.

DEATH WISHES, HOLOCAUST, INFANTICIDAL INTROJECT, PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHOLOGICAL INFANTICIDE, PSYCHOTHERAPY, SCHIZOPHRENIA, SIGMUND FREUD, TRAUMATOLOGY

In this article, the author explores the complex controversies surrounding the aetiology of the schizophrenic psychoses. After reviewing the historical literature, the author discusses the ongoing debate between the opposing biopathological and psychoanalytical models of causation. In particular, he examines the considerable, but often neglected, body of evidence in support of a theory of the traumatogenic origin of the severe psychoses, including not only clinical but also empirical psychopathological research, especially findings from Holocaust studies. Drawing upon his own psychoanalytical work with psychotic patients over many decades, the author proposes a theory of aetiology based on the widespread occurrence of conscious and unconscious parental death wishes in the early histories of individuals who later became diagnosed as schizophrenic. He traces the development of his concepts of ‘psychological infanticide’ and the ‘infanticidal introject’, providing clinical illustrations of the ways in which early death wishes towards babies and children impact upon the subsequent onset of psychopathology.
